caption: Figure 1. Model Size vs. ImageNet Accuracy. All numbers are for single-crop, single-model. Our EfficientNets significantly outperform other ConvNets. caption: Figure 2. Model Scaling. (a) is a baseline network example; (b)-(d) are conventional scaling that only increases one dimension of network width, depth, or resolution. (e) is our proposed compound scaling method that uniformly scales all three dimensions with a fixed ratio.
description:
## Description
This figure illustrates different scaling methods for convolutional neural networks. It shows five panels: (a) baseline, (b) width scaling, (c) depth scaling, (d) resolution scaling, and (e) compound scaling. Each panel depicts a network architecture with varying dimensions. The baseline network has a fixed number of channels, width, depth, and resolution. Width scaling increases the number of channels, depth scaling increases the number of layers, resolution scaling increases the input image size, and compound scaling uniformly scales all dimensions.

## Text in figure
(a) baseline: #channels, layer_i, resolution HxW
(b) width scaling: wider, #channels, layer_i, resolution HxW
(c) depth scaling: deeper, #channels, layer_i, resolution HxW
(d) resolution scaling: higher resolution, #channels, layer_i, resolution HxW
(e) compound scaling: wider, deeper, higher resolution, #channels, layer_i, resolution HxW

caption: Figure 3. Scaling Up a Baseline Model with Different Network Width ( w ), Depth ( d ), and Resolution ( r ) Coefficients. Bigger networks with larger width, depth, or resolution tend to achieve higher accuracy, but the accuracy gain quickly saturate after reaching 80%, demonstrating the limitation of single dimension scaling. description:
Description: The figure shows six scatter plots comparing the number of model parameters (log-scale) with transfer learning accuracy on various datasets. Each plot represents a different dataset, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Birds, Stanford Cars, Flowers, FGVC Aircraft, Oxford-IIIT Pets, and Food-101. The series include DenseNet-201, ResNet-50, Inception-v3, ResNet-152, DenseNet-121, and NASNet-A. NASNet-A consistently shows the highest accuracy across all datasets, while DenseNet-121 has the lowest accuracy in most cases.
